name: scope-appropriate-project-setup
description: Chooses simple project structure without imposing an architecture questionnaire.
prompt: I'm starting a new Go web service project. Set up the directory structure for me.
trap: Blocks routine setup on architecture and DI questions or silently adds mandatory skill-loading configuration.

assertions.text: Uses request context and existing conventions to choose a simple starting structure
Asks only about missing requirements that materially affect structure
Avoids imposing unnecessary architecture layers
Does not install DI libraries or add agent configuration as a side effect
Keeps small projects minimally structured

name: cmd-directory-minimal-logic
description: Tests whether the model keeps cmd/ main.go minimal with no business logic
prompt: I'm organizing a Go project with an HTTP server. Here's my cmd/server/main.go that has 200 lines including request parsing, database queries, and response formatting. Is this OK?
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept the large main.go or only suggest minor improvements. Substantial reusable logic can move into focused internal packages; cmd packages may contain multiple files and tests.

assertions.text: Says business logic does NOT belong in cmd/server/main.go
Says cmd/ should contain minimal logic: parse flags, wire dependencies, call Run()
Recommends moving business logic to internal/ or pkg/
main.go should primarily do dependency wiring and startup
Extracts substantial reusable or independently testable logic without requiring a fixed main-package file count

name: no-src-utils-helpers-common
description: Tests whether the model avoids Java-style src/ directory and generic package names
prompt:
I'm organizing my Go project. I created these directories: src/ for source code, utils/ for utility functions, helpers/ for helper functions, and common/ for shared code. Here's my structure:

```
myproject/
  src/
    main.go
  utils/
    string_utils.go
  helpers/
    http_helper.go
  common/
    types.go
```

Does this look good?
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept some of these (especially utils/) as reasonable. The skill explicitly calls out src/, utils/, helpers/, common/ as anti-patterns.

assertions.text: Explains a separate src directory is unnecessary in ordinary module layouts, not prohibited by Go.
Rejects utils/ as a generic package name
Rejects helpers/ as a generic package name
Rejects common/ as a generic package name
Suggests domain-specific package names instead (e.g. format/, stringconv/)
Allows a root main package for a small command or cmd/{name} when separating entrypoints helps

name: module-naming-conventions
description: Distinguishes valid module paths from naming preferences.
prompt:
I'm initializing a new Go module. Which of these module names is correct?

1. `module myproject`
2. `module github.com/jdoe/MyProject`
3. `module github.com/jdoe/my-project`
4. `module github.com/jdoe/my_project`
5. `module utils`
trap: Rejects legal module paths or renames a repository path based on a style preference.

assertions.text: Option 3 is conventional if it matches the actual source repository.
Local-only main modules can use myproject; remotely fetched module paths normally need a domain.
Uppercase letters are legal; preserve the actual repository case.
Underscores are legal in module paths; hyphens are a preference, not a toolchain requirement.
Vanity domains and subdirectory/v2 paths are valid; the module path need not literally equal a hosting URL.

name: internal-vs-pkg-decision
description: Tests whether the model correctly decides between internal/ and pkg/ based on export requirements
prompt: I'm building a Go project with both a web service and a shared logging library that other teams want to import. I also have some private request parsing code. Where should I put each?
trap: Without the skill, the model may put everything in internal/ or everything in pkg/. The skill says internal/ for non-exported, pkg/ only when code is useful to external consumers.

assertions.text: Puts the public library at the root or an importable subpackage; pkg/ is optional.
Puts the private request parsing code in internal/ (not exported)
Explains internal import visibility is limited to the parent directory tree, not universally the whole module.
Explains pkg/ has no special toolchain meaning.
Service/business logic goes in internal/ by default

name: workspace-when-to-use
description: Tests whether the model recommends go.work only for multi-module scenarios, not single-module projects
prompt: I have a single Go module project (one go.mod) with about 10 packages. A colleague suggested I add go.work for better organization. Should I?
trap: Without the skill, the model may recommend go.work for any multi-package project. The skill says don't use workspaces for single-module projects or simple applications.

assertions.text: Recommends AGAINST using go.work for a single-module project
Explains that go.work is for multiple related Go modules that import each other
Mentions that a single module with multiple packages does not need a workspace
Lists valid use cases: monorepo with separate modules, local cross-module development

name: twelve-factor-app-conventions
description: Tests whether the model applies 12-Factor App principles for Go services
prompt: I'm building a Go microservice that reads its database URL from a config.yaml file checked into the repository. It writes logs to a file at /var/log/myapp.log. Is this a good approach?
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept file-based config and log files as reasonable. The skill says to follow 12-Factor: config via environment variables, logs to stdout.

assertions.text: Recommends reading database URL from environment variables, not a checked-in config file
Recommends writing logs to stdout, not to a file
References or describes 12-Factor App principles
Mentions that sensitive values (like DB URLs) should never be in config files committed to source control
Explains WHY: environment-based config allows different values per deployment without code changes

name: library-layout-no-cmd
description: Tests whether the model uses the correct layout for a Go library (no cmd/, public packages at root level)
prompt: I'm creating a Go library for other developers to import (a logging package). How should I structure the project? Should I put the code in cmd/ or pkg/?
trap: Without the skill, the model may use the application layout (cmd/, internal/, pkg/) for a library. The skill shows that libraries put public API in root-level directories, no cmd/ unless example binaries.

assertions.text: Uses a root public package or suitable public subpackage; pkg/ is optional, cmd packages are commands.
No cmd/ directory (unless for example binaries)
Uses internal/ for private implementation details
Adds executable examples only when useful; test examples can live alongside the library.
Structure follows the library layout pattern, not the application layout pattern

name: test-file-colocation
description: Tests whether the model co-locates test files with the code they test
prompt: I'm organizing tests in my Go project. Should I create a separate tests/ directory at the root to hold all test files, or should I put them somewhere else?
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept a centralized tests/ directory (common in Python/Java). The skill says co-locate _test.go files with the code they test.

assertions.text: Recommends co-locating test files with the code they test (same directory)
Test files use the _test.go suffix
Does NOT recommend a centralized tests/ directory for unit tests
Mentions testdata/ directory for test fixtures
Distinguishes between white-box (same package) and black-box (package_test) testing approaches

name: config-sensitive-values-env-only
description: Protects secrets through deployment controls, not a blanket file ban.
prompt: I'm setting up configuration for my Go service using Viper. I want to put the database password, API keys, and JWT secret in my config.yaml for convenience. Then I'll use mapstructure tags to load them. Good idea?

assertions.text: Keeps secrets out of committed ordinary config; access-controlled secret files can be appropriate.
Uses the deployment's secret transport, including environment variables or mounted secret files.
May suggest a secret manager as an alternative
Config files are acceptable for non-sensitive values (port, log level, etc.)
Explains exposure and access controls without claiming environment variables are inherently safer than files.

name: multiple-binaries-cmd-structure
description: Tests whether the model creates separate subdirectories in cmd/ for each binary
prompt: My Go project needs three binaries: an API server, a CLI tool, and a database migration utility. How should I organize the cmd/ directory?
trap: Without the skill, the model may put all three in a single cmd/main.go with subcommands. The skill shows separate subdirectories in cmd/ for each binary.

assertions.text: Creates separate subdirectories: cmd/server/, cmd/cli/, cmd/migrate/ (or similar names)
Each subdirectory has its own main.go with package main
Each binary can be built independently (go build ./cmd/server, etc.)
Mentions go build ./cmd/... to build all binaries at once
Business logic is in internal/, not duplicated across cmd/ directories
